tasks.title: The product says what it does with your data, and can delete it.
tasks.description: This task adds the terms, the privacy notice, a real account deletion, and a support channel.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. The public pages of the site.
2. The data model and a deletion endpoint.
3. A support address and a changelog.

DEFINITIONS
- Processor: a service that handles personal data on the product's behalf.
- Deletion: removal of every row belonging to an account, verified.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Notice
A privacy notice shall name the processors actually used.

R2 — Terms
Terms shall be published and linked at sign-in.

R3 — Export
A person shall be able to export every workspace they own.

R4 — Deletion
Deleting an account shall remove its rows, and the removal shall be verified.

R5 — Support
A support address and a response expectation shall be published.

R6 — Changes recorded
A changelog shall record user-visible changes.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 — R3: Export an account's workspaces; the file opens and contains every entity.
V2 — R4: Delete an account; a query finds no rows, and a second sign-in creates a fresh account.
V3 — R1: The notice's processor list matches the vendors actually configured.
V4 — R2: The sign-in surface links the terms.
tasks.complexityReasoning: Public pages, a verified deletion across every table, and support with a changelog.

tasks.title: A board has a history of its own: what moved, what changed, and who.
tasks.description: This task gives every board a history view, derived from the entries the workspace already holds.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

Task 116 put an author on every new entry, and a move has always carried the board it happened on.
Between them the entries already describe a board's life; what is missing is a screen that reads
them, and one honest decision about what a board can and cannot know.

SCOPE
1. A board view — `components/BoardHistory.tsx`, the view switch, and `view=history` in `lib/url.ts`.
2. `domain/history.ts` — deriving one board's entries from the items it holds, newest first.
3. The lane actions in the store, for R4 (board-design events are not recorded today).

DEFINITIONS
- Board history: the entries that concern one board — its moves, and the changes to the items it
  holds — newest first.
- Move entry: a log entry of kind `moved`, which carries the board it happened on, the lanes and
  the stages as they were.
- Item change: any other entry on an item. It carries a time, a kind, a note and (since task 116)
  an author — but not a board.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — A place
The board's history shall be a view of the board, at its own URL (`view=history`), reachable from
the board's navigation, and board-specific like every other board view.

R2 — Moves, exactly
Every move recorded on this board shall appear, with the lanes and stages as they were. The entry
carries them, so a lane renamed or removed later cannot rewrite the past.

R3 — Changes, honestly bounded
Changes to the items this board holds shall appear too, and the screen shall say what it cannot
know: an item can sit on several boards, and an edit records no board. The task shall choose one of
two honest answers and write down why: record the board on new entries (so the future is exact),
or label changes as the item's own history rather than the board's.

R4 — The board's own design
Splitting, adding, renaming or removing a lane, and changing a WIP limit, are not recorded at all
today. A board's history that omits them is missing its most consequential events. They shall be
recorded, with the same who and when, and shown in the same view.

R5 — Nothing invented
An entry from before identities existed shall show no author. A deleted item takes its history
with it. The screen shall show what exists rather than filling the gaps.

R6 — Derived, not stored
The view shall read the items' logs. It shall not add a second place where history lives: one
workspace, one record, however many ways it is read.

VERIFICATION

V1 — R1: A deep link to `view=history` opens it, and the board's navigation names it.
V2 — R2: Move a card, rename the lane it left, then open the history: the entry names the lane as
it was, with the person's name beside it.
V3 — R3: With an item on two boards, a change made while the other board was in front appears —
and is described in the terms the task chose.
V4 — R4: Split a lane; the split appears in the history with its author and time.
V5 — R5: An old entry renders without an author; delete an item and its entries leave with it.
V6 — R6: `localStorage` gains no history key; the view reads what the workspace already holds.

CANCELLED — 2026-10-21
A card can sit on several boards, so its history is the card's, not the board's. A board-level view
would have to attribute an edit to a board the person may not have been looking at — a record that
lies about what it saw. The entries are already per item, and the card's own Activity tab is where
the model puts them: the feature this task was reaching for already exists in the right place.

What the task noticed along the way is a separate question and not a task: a board's own design
changes — splitting, renaming or removing a lane, changing a WIP limit — are recorded nowhere. That
is a gap in the *board's* record, not the card's, and it should be decided on its own terms.

tasks.title: The project runs on a machine its owner controls.
tasks.description: This task packages the portable server as something a team can run: a Docker image, a compose file, a first run that makes the first account the owner, and the environment it documents.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. A multi-stage Dockerfile: build the client, copy the server, run the Node entry on a small base
   image.
2. A compose file: one service, one volume, one port.
3. A first run that applies the migrations, makes the first account the owner, and needs no manual
   SQL.
4. Configuration by environment, documented in one place: the database path, the public URL, the
   providers, the mail relay.
5. A health endpoint, and a README section a self-hoster can follow without reading this repository.

DEFINITIONS
- Self-hosted instance: one deployment a team runs, on a machine they own, with one workspace.
- First run: the state an instance is in before anyone has signed in.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One command
Bringing an instance up shall be one command after a checkout, and the image shall build from the
repository alone.

R2 — No manual setup
The first run shall apply the migrations, create the storage the server needs and start answering —
no SQL typed by hand, no seed script to remember.

R3 — The first account owns the instance
The first person to sign in shall become the owner, and the instance shall refuse a second owner
without an explicit handover.

R4 — Configuration is environment
Every deployment-specific value shall arrive as an environment variable and be documented in one
place: the database, the public URL, the providers, the mail relay.

R5 — Data outlives the container
The database and any uploaded file shall live on a volume, and removing the container shall not
remove them.

R6 — Honest readiness
A health endpoint shall say whether the instance can serve, and the app shall say when it cannot —
the honesty `persist()` already gives the browser.

R7 — Nothing hostile by default
The image shall run as a non-root user, expose no debugging port, and ship no default credentials.

R8 — Say what SQLite means
The documentation shall say plainly that a file-backed database serves one instance: scaling out
means Postgres, not a second container on the same file, and backing up means copying the volume.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 — R1: from a clean clone, build and start with one command; the app answers.
V2 — R2, R5: stop and remove the container; start it again on the same volume; the workspace is there.
V3 — R3: sign in as the first person; the admin surface is theirs. Invite a second; they are not an owner.
V4 — R4: change the public URL and a provider through the environment; both take effect.
V5 — R6: break the database path; the health endpoint says so rather than the app failing quietly.
V6 — R7: inspect the running container; its user is not root.
V7 — R8: read the README as someone who has only just heard of the project; the limit and the backup are stated, not implied.
tasks.expansionPrompt: (1) the Dockerfile and the Node entry in the image; (2) compose, the volume and the config; (3) first run, migrations and the owner; (4) the health endpoint and the README a self-hoster follows.
tasks.complexityReasoning: Packaging rather than invention: the server and schema already exist, so the work is an image, a volume, a first run, a health check and documentation honest enough to follow without the repository open.

tasks.title: The server has a shape before it has a route.
tasks.description: This task builds the portable HTTP seam — one Hono app, two entry files, one database interface — so that 117's first route and 118's first table are written once and run in both places.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

SCOPE
1. A Hono application in `server/` that is the whole API: one `fetch` handler, no bindings.
2. A `Database` interface, with two implementations — D1, and a driver over a SQLite file.
3. `worker/index.ts` as the Cloudflare entry: bindings in, `app.fetch` out, nothing else.
4. `server/index.node.ts` as the Node entry: a port, a database path, `serve(app.fetch)`.
5. A health route that answers on both, and static assets served by both.
6. A second CI job that boots the Node entry and replays the API paths the e2e suite uses.
7. The existing `/api/errors` endpoint moved onto the seam — the first route proven in both places —
   with the pure parser beside it in `server/`.

DEFINITIONS
- Entry: the only file that knows which runtime it is on.
- Seam: the four things that differ between deployments — the entry file, the database binding,
  static assets, and the live channel.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — One handler
The API shall be one `fetch` handler. A Worker shall export it; a Node process shall serve it.

R2 — Bindings at the edge of the code
`cloudflare:*` imports, `D1Database`, `env.ASSETS` and `cf-connecting-ip` shall appear only in
`worker/`. `server/` shall compile and run without them.

R3 — The database behind an interface
Every statement shall go through `Database` — `all`, `get`, `run`, `batch` — with two
implementations: D1, and a SQLite file in the Node entry. No statement shall depend on an API only
one of them has.

R4 — Assets on both
The built client shall be served by the Worker's asset router and by the Node entry, with the same
single-page fallback, so every place in the app is a URL on both.

R5 — Health
`GET /api/health` shall answer on both entries, and shall say whether the database can be reached
rather than answering 200 regardless.

R6 — The second runtime is tested
CI shall boot the Node entry against a temporary database and replay the API paths the e2e suite
uses, so a route that works on one runtime and not the other fails the build.

R7 — No behaviour change
The app shall behave exactly as it does today. This task adds a shape, not a feature.

R8 — The endpoint that exists comes with us
`/api/errors` shall move onto the seam rather than sit beside it: the same statuses — 204, 400, 413,
429, 503 when the database is absent — the same hourly cap, and the same salted address hash. It
shall lose its direct D1 access and reach the database through `Database`. Because it is the first
route, it shall gain the test it never had: today only its parser is tested, not the endpoint.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-21
`server/` holds the whole API as one Hono handler. `Runtime` names the three things that are
genuinely per-runtime — the database, the client's address, and the salt — so no route reads a
binding. `worker/index.ts` is the Cloudflare entry over `worker/d1.ts`; `server/index.node.ts` is the
Node entry over `node:sqlite`, serving the built client with the SPA fallback.

`/api/errors` moved onto the seam and gained the test it never had: seven cases against a real
database built from the real migrations. `/api/health` asks the database rather than assuming it.

`npm run portable` fails the build if a Cloudflare binding appears in `server/`, and
`npm run smoke:node` boots the Node entry on a temporary database and uses the API. CI runs both.
Hono is the framework; the contract underneath it is `Request` to `Response`, as
`docs/server-runtime.md` argues, so the framework stays replaceable.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 — R1, R4: open the built app on both entries; the board works on each, deep links included.
V2 — R2: CI searches `server/` for `cloudflare:` and binding types; it finds nothing.
V3 — R3: point each implementation at a temporary database; the same statement answers the same on both.
V4 — R5: `GET /api/health` on both; remove the database and it says so rather than answering 200.
V5 — R6: break one route on the Node entry only; CI fails.
V6 — R7: the existing unit and e2e suites pass unchanged.
V7 — R8: a report is accepted on both entries and stored; an oversized body is refused with 413; with no
database configured it answers 503; the hourly cap still answers 429.
tasks.expansionPrompt: (1) the Hono app and the health route in `server/`; (2) the `Database` interface with a D1 implementation; (3) the SQLite-file implementation and the Node entry; (4) static assets and the SPA fallback on both; (5) the CI job that boots Node and replays the API paths.
tasks.complexityReasoning: A small amount of code with a large blast radius: every later route and table is written on this seam, so getting the boundary wrong is expensive and getting it right is cheap. The CI lane is what keeps it honest.

tasks.title: A board's dashboard leads with the work that needs attention, and the cards behind every number.
tasks.description: The dashboard's first section becomes a count band of attention signals over the board's unfinished work — overdue, stale, unassigned, no priority, no estimate — with a review list beneath it holding exactly the items behind those counts, so a reader can go from a number to the card in one click.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository.

The dashboard today is an initiative table and a time-in-column table. A team board usually has no initiatives placed on it, so its dashboard is nearly empty, and the first question anyone opens a dashboard with — "what is at risk of being forgotten?" — has no answer on any board. This task gives every board dashboard a first section, modelled on the "Needs attention" band and "Items to review" list in the supplied reference: a count band over the work the board renders, and a review list of exactly the items behind those counts.

SCOPE
1. `src/domain/attention.ts` — the derivation, pure and unit tested.
2. `src/domain/attention.test.ts` — the boundaries and the invariants.
3. `src/components/ManagementDashboard.tsx` — the band and the list at the top of the dashboard, above the initiative table.
4. `src/lib/colors.ts` — only if a genuine reuse gap appears. The badge set is not to be reinvented.

DEFINITIONS
- Attention item: an item this board renders and has not finished — not archived, and not in a Done stage.
- Signal: one reason an attention item deserves a closer look. The set is closed in this task; nothing else is invented.
- The board's work: the cards placed on a board that renders a cards workflow; the initiatives placed on a board that does not.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Derived, never stored
Every signal shall be computed from state the model already keeps — the placements, the lane stamps, the assignees, the priority, the size and the target dates. Nothing shall be written onto an item, no persisted field shall be added, and there shall be no persist version bump or migration. `attention.ts` shall take the graph, the board id, the issue types and `now`, and return the items and the counts; the component shall compute nothing of its own.

R2 — Six signals, each defined once
The band shall carry these tiles, in this order:

- **Unfinished** — the population itself: cards placed on this board, not archived, whose stage is not Done. Every other count is a subset of this one, which is an invariant to test.
- **Overdue** — `isOverdue(item, resolved)` from `filters.ts`, the same predicate the filter panel uses. A finished or archived card is never overdue.
- **Stale** — committed work (Not Started or In Progress) whose placement carries a `laneEnteredAt` older than `STALE_AFTER_DAYS`. A card with no stamp is *not* stale: an unknown last movement is not the same as no movement, exactly as `initiativeHealth` already argues. The threshold shall be read from the constant, never typed into the component; the subtitle shall name the real threshold ("No movement for 7+ days"), not the 30 in the reference screenshot.
- **Unassigned** — no assignees, matching the `unassigned` filter exactly, so the number and the filtered board cannot disagree.
- **No priority** — `priority` is undefined. Priority is a judgement the team makes, so its absence is a reviewable gap rather than an error.
- **No estimate** — `size` is undefined, on **cards only**. An initiative has no estimate by design, so an initiative is never counted against one; on a board with no cards workflow the tile is absent, not zero.

R3 — Coordination boards read their own work
A board with no cards workflow shall run the same section over its own initiatives rather than over cards: Overdue from the target date against the derived rollup bucket, Stale and Unowned from `initiativeHealth` (whose `stale` and `unowned` rules already read the work below), No priority from the item, and no No estimate tile at all. The shape, the ordering, the band and the list shall be identical, so the dashboard reads the same way on a team board and a programme board.

R4 — One computation, two surfaces
The band and the review list shall read one array. A tile's number shall always equal the number of rows carrying that signal, and a row's signal chips shall be the same objects the counts were taken from. This is asserted in a unit test, so the heading and the list can never tell different stories.

R5 — Every count is a door
Clicking a tile shall narrow the review list to the items carrying that signal — view state only, never the board's saved filters and never a store write. Choosing the selected tile again, or an "All" affordance, shall restore the full list. Clicking a row shall open that item with the store's existing `openItem`, so a number can become the card in one click. The tiles shall be real buttons with accessible names, not divs with click handlers.

R6 — Order that puts the worst first
Rows shall be ordered by number of signals, descending; then by known age, descending, with unknown ages last; then by title, case-insensitively. Nothing else. A reader should be able to stop after the first row and still have seen the worst item.

R7 — Quiet, honest, and never nagging
When no item carries a signal, the section shall say so in one calm sentence and draw no band. An unknown age shall render as an em dash, never `0d` and never "new". Nothing shall be auto-flagged, auto-moved, auto-assigned or notified; this surface only reports what is already true, which is the same contract as the health column and the aging cue.

R8 — One vocabulary
The signal chips shall reuse `FLAG_BADGE_SHAPE` and `FLAG_BADGE` from `lib/colors.ts` — risk for Overdue, watch for the rest — and `STAGE_LABELS` for any fallback status. Age and overdue shall come from `ageDays` and `isOverdue`, not a second implementation. Each chip shall carry its rule's own `why` as a `title`, the way `HealthFlagInfo` already does, so a badge explains itself in words. No new badge palette, no second notion of stale.

R9 — The list's own columns
The review table shall carry Item (type colour and title), Status (the lane the card sits in, falling back to the stage's label), Age (whole days in the current lane), and Signals (the chips). It shall sit directly beneath the band, titled "Items to review", and wear the same bordered white card as the tables already there.

R10 — The export does not change
`dashboardCsv` shall keep exporting the initiative rows exactly as it does today. The attention section is a reading surface, not a second export; adding attention rows would change the meaning of a file that already has one.

DELIVERED — 2026-10-21
`src/domain/attention.ts` derives the band and the review list from one row array: each row is an item the board renders and has not finished, with its lane path, its known age, and the signals it carries. The counts are taken from that array, so a tile and the rows behind it cannot disagree, and `hasEstimate` says whether the No estimate tile exists at all.

The population follows the app's own rule rather than the presence of a lane tree: `isAggregating` decides, so a programme or portfolio board reads its initiatives through `initiativeHealth` — stale and unowned in that rule's own words — and a team board reads its cards. Staleness reuses `STALE_AFTER_DAYS` and says nothing without a lane stamp; overdue reuses `isOverdue`; the list's status is the lane path, with the stage as fallback. No store field, no migration, and `dashboardCsv` is untouched.

The dashboard leads with Needs attention: tile buttons (`aria-pressed`) narrow the Items to review table, Show all clears them, Unfinished shows the whole population, and a row opens the item. A board with no signals draws a sentence instead of a band, and an unknown age is an em dash.

`attention.test.ts` covers each signal's boundary, unknown stamps, Done and archived exclusions, the counts-equal-rows invariant, ordering, the initiative path, and the absent estimate tile. The full suite (430 tests), typecheck, lint, scan, build and the bundle-size check pass.

FOLLOW-UP — 2026-10-22
The initiative overview now sits between the Needs attention band and Items to review. Each review row also carries an Open on board action (an external-link button in its own column): the row still opens the drawer, while the action leaves the dashboard for the board with that item open.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 — R1: unit tests in `attention.test.ts` build a graph by hand and assert every signal from it. Nothing on an item changes after the computation.

V2 — R2: boundaries, one test each — a card due yesterday is overdue and one due tomorrow is not; a card exactly `STALE_AFTER_DAYS` old is stale and one day short is not; a card with no `laneEnteredAt` is never stale; a Done or archived card appears in no count; a Backlog card is not stale but can be unassigned; a card with `size: 0` has an estimate while one with `size: undefined` does not.

V3 — R3: a graph with no cards workflow yields initiative rows; the estimate tile is absent rather than 0, and the stale count agrees with `initiativeHealth` for the same graph.

V4 — R4: for each tile, the number equals the length of the rows selecting it, and every count is at most Unfinished.

V5 — R5: clicking a tile narrows the list and clicking it again restores it; the board's saved filters are unchanged; clicking a row sets the store's selected item.

V6 — R6: a fixture with equal and unequal signal counts, known and unknown ages, and two same-aged titles asserts the exact row order.

V7 — R7: an empty board renders the sentence and no tiles; a card without a placement stamp shows an em dash.

V8 — R8: the staleness threshold and the overdue predicate are imported from the domain; changing `STALE_AFTER_DAYS` changes the subtitle without touching the component.

V9 — R9: the dashboard for a seeded board shows the band first, then Items to review, then the existing initiative and time-in-column tables.

V10 — R10: the dashboard CSV output is byte-identical before and after this change for the same graph.

V11 — `npm run scan`, `npm test` and `npm run build` pass.
tasks.expansionPrompt: (1) the pure `attention.ts` derivation over cards, with the six signals and the counts-equal-rows invariant, plus `attention.test.ts`; (2) the count band as buttons, with its selected state narrowing the list; (3) the Items to review table with status, age and signal chips, and row-open; (4) the coordination-board path over initiatives, wired into `ManagementDashboard` above the existing tables.
tasks.complexityReasoning: The signals are cheap to derive because the predicates already exist; the care is in the invariants — one population, counts equal to rows, unknown ages never accused — and in making a coordination board read the same section without inventing an estimate for an initiative.

tasks.title: One permission model decides who may do what.
tasks.description: A single pure domain function turns a viewer, editor or administrator role into an answer for every action in the app, so the UI and the API cannot disagree. Today members.role is decorative: it is returned by /api/auth/session and printed in the account menu, but nothing checks it.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/admin.md section 3.2 before starting.

SCOPE
1. A new pure module, src/domain/roles.ts.
2. The role vocabulary and the action vocabulary.
3. The permission matrix, in one place.
4. One unit test per role x action pair.

DEFINITIONS
- Role: viewer, editor or administrator. Internally 'viewer' | 'editor' | 'admin'.
- Action: a named thing a person can do, e.g. 'item.write', 'board.design'.
- Matrix: the single table that says which role may take which action.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Types
Export Role, Action and can(role, action): boolean. Action is a closed union, not a string.

R2 - Matrix
The matrix is exactly docs/admin.md section 3.2:
- Viewer: read boards/cards/initiatives/objectives/metrics/activity, search, filter, export a board, comment, see names in the people directory.
- Editor: everything Viewer can, plus create/edit/move/rank a card, create an initiative, set parent, dependency, tag, checklist, attribute an initiative to an objective, create a board from a template.
- Administrator: everything Editor can, plus board design (split/add/rename/reorder/remove a lane, orientation), WIP limits and policy, board settings and bindings, archive/delete a board, delete a card, remove a template, import a workspace, restore a snapshot, create/revoke a share link, manage workspace members and settings.

R3 - The two debatable rows
Board design is Administrator-only. Attribution is Editor-allowed while creating/deleting objectives and key results is Administrator-only. Record both in a comment beside the matrix.

R4 - Display metadata
Export a ROLES list with each role's display label and one sentence a person can read in an invite dialog.

R5 - Purity
No import from src/store.ts, src/components, server or any browser API. This module is unit tested and is the only place the matrix lives.

R6 - Unknown input
An unrecognised role or action answers false. The switch is exhaustive so the compiler notices a new action that has no decision.

OUT OF SCOPE
Enforcement (task 133), schema (task 132), custom roles, groups, passkeys, API tokens.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - Every role x action pair has one assertion; the test names the pair.
V2 - Viewer cannot item.write, board.design, workspace.members or workspace.share.
V3 - Editor can item.write and item.attribute; cannot board.design or workspace.members.
V4 - Administrator can every action in the union.
V5 - can('nonsense' as Role, 'item.read') is false.
V6 - ROLES has exactly three entries, each with a label and a description.

tasks.title: The schema separates instance access from workspace authority.
tasks.description: A migration splits the overloaded members table into instance_members and workspace_members, grows the account and session records, reissues invitations as hashed tokens, and adds the audit table. Existing members rows keep their authority.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 4. This is the schema half of backlog task 122; 132-136 and 142 together satisfy its role, invitation, removal and ownership clauses.

SCOPE
1. migrations/0003_people.sql, plain SQLite, applicable unchanged to D1 and a file.
2. Account fields, instance membership, workspace membership, sessions, invitations, audit.
3. A data migration for every row that exists today.
4. First-run bootstrap that makes the first person an administrator.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Account
users gains avatar_url, timezone, language, status ('active' | 'inactive', default active), last_seen_at, updated_at. status is a CHECK constraint or a documented closed set.

R2 - Two axes
instance_members(user_id PK, role 'admin'|'member', created_at).
workspace_members(workspace_id, user_id, role 'viewer'|'editor'|'admin', invited_by, created_at, PK(workspace_id,user_id)).
The two are never collapsed into one column.

R3 - Invitations
Rebuild invites: id, email, role, token_hash UNIQUE, invited_by, created_at, expires_at, accepted_at, revoked_at. SQLite cannot change the primary key in place, so create the new table, copy what can be copied, drop the old one in one batch.

R4 - Sessions
sessions gains user_agent, ip_hash, last_seen_at, revoked_at. The token hash stays the primary key.

R5 - Audit
audit_events(id, at, actor_id, action, target_type, target_id, data JSON text, ip_hash) with indexes on at and (actor_id, at).

R6 - Existing rows
Every members row becomes an instance_members row: owner -> admin, member -> member.
Every owner also becomes a workspace admin; every member becomes a workspace editor (preserves today's ability to edit).
Old invites cannot become links. Reissue them with a fresh token on first read, or drop and re-invite; document the choice in the migration comment.

R7 - First run
When the first account is created, instance_members.role = admin and workspace_members.role = admin are written in the same batch as the workspace row. There must be no moment where an instance has an account but no administrator.

R8 - Both runtimes
The migration runs through Database.batch on D1 and the Node file driver. A test opens a fixture database at the old shape, applies the migration, and asserts the mapping.

OUT OF SCOPE
Route enforcement (133), access policy (134), UI.

SPLIT — 2026-10-22
Three subtasks, following the requirement groups rather than the table list: the two axes (132.1),
the records that hang off them (132.2), and the move of what already exists (132.3). The migration
is the next free number, not the `0003` this task's scope named — 0003 is the workspace.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - A fixture at the 0002 shape with one owner and two members migrates with roles admin/admin, member/editor.
V2 - The unique index on invites.token_hash rejects a duplicate.
V3 - A workspace_members row has exactly one role and cannot be duplicated for the same pair.
V4 - Deleting a user leaves audit_events readable with actor_id NULL (ON DELETE SET NULL).
V5 - status defaults to active for existing users and rejects an unknown value.
V6 - Applying the migration twice is safe or fails loudly without partial state.
V7 - The static build still boots; nothing in src reads the new tables.

subtasks.title: Accounts, the two axes, and the first run.
subtasks.description: SYSTEM
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/admin.md sections 3.1 and 4.

SCOPE
1. The account fields on `users`.
2. `instance_members` and `workspace_members` — two tables, two questions.
3. The first run, which must leave an instance with an administrator.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — The account
`users` shall gain `avatar_url`, `timezone`, `language`, `status` (`active` | `inactive`, default
active), `last_seen_at` and `updated_at`. `status` shall be a CHECK constraint or a documented
closed set, not free text.

R2 — Two axes, never one column
`instance_members(user_id PK, role 'admin' | 'member', created_at)` answers "may this person sign in
at all". `workspace_members(workspace_id, user_id, role 'viewer' | 'editor' | 'admin', invited_by,
created_at, PK(workspace_id, user_id))` answers "what may they do here". They shall not be collapsed
into one role, because they are different questions with different answers.

R3 — The first run
When the first account is created, `instance_members.role = admin` and the workspace's
`workspace_members.role = admin` shall be written in the same batch as the workspace row. There
shall be no moment at which an instance has an account and no administrator.

R4 — The old table keeps its meaning until it is migrated
`members` shall not be dropped here; task 132.3 moves its rows. Until then both exist and the read
prefers the new tables.

R5 — Both runtimes
The statements shall be plain SQLite and go through `Database.batch`, so the migration applies
unchanged to D1 and to a file.

VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: a user row with `status = 'banned'` is refused by the database.
V2 — R2: a person can be an instance member without a workspace row, and a workspace member without
being an instance administrator.
V3 — R3: on a fresh database the first sign-in leaves exactly one admin in each table.
V4 — R5: the migration runs on both drivers in the round-trip test.

subtasks.title: Invitations as tokens, sessions as records, and the audit table.
subtasks.description: SYSTEM
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/admin.md sections 3.5, 3.6 and 4.

SCOPE
1. The `invites` rebuild.
2. The session columns.
3. `audit_events`.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — An invitation is a single-use token
`invites` shall be rebuilt as `(id, email, role, token_hash UNIQUE, invited_by, created_at,
expires_at, accepted_at, revoked_at)`. The token shall exist only in the link that is handed over;
the table shall hold its hash, so a copy of the database is not a set of working invitations.

R2 — Rebuilt in one batch
SQLite cannot change a primary key in place, so the new table shall be created, what can be copied
shall be copied, and the old one dropped in a single batch — never across two statements a crash can
split.

R3 — Sessions are records
`sessions` shall gain `user_agent`, `ip_hash`, `last_seen_at` and `revoked_at`. The token hash stays
the primary key, and revocation shall be a column rather than a delete, so "sign out everywhere" and
the audit can both see it.

R4 — The audit is append-only
`audit_events(id, at, actor_id, action, target_type, target_id, data JSON text, ip_hash)` with an
index on `at` and on `(actor_id, at)`. Nothing shall update or delete a row: it is a record, and a
record that can be edited is not one.

R5 — No workspace in it
The audit row shall name the actor, the action and the target. It shall not carry a card's title, a
person's address beyond the hashed IP, or anything else that would turn a log into a copy of the
workspace.

VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: the same token cannot be accepted twice, and an expired one is refused.
V2 — R2: a database with an old `invites` row migrates without a half-written table.
V3 — R3: a revoked session cannot be used, and the row is still there.
V4 — R4: nothing in the code paths updates or deletes an audit row, and the migration adds the
trigger that would stop it if anything tried.

subtasks.title: The migration of what exists, and the test that says it worked.
subtasks.description: SYSTEM
subtasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline, the application in this repository. Read docs/admin.md section 4, requirements R6-R8.

SCOPE
1. The data migration from `members` and the old `invites`.
2. A fixture database at the old shape.
3. The documented choice about old invitations.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 — Every member keeps their ability
Every `members` row shall become an `instance_members` row (`owner` -> `admin`, `member` ->
`member`), and every owner shall also become a workspace `admin` while every member becomes a
workspace `editor` — which is what they can do today, so nobody loses a capability in the move.

R2 — Old invitations are honoured or explicitly dropped
The old table has no token, so an old invitation cannot become a link. The migration shall either
reissue a fresh token on first read or drop the row, and it shall say which in a comment beside the
statement. Silently keeping a row that can never be accepted is not an option.

R3 — A test at the old shape
A test shall open a database created by the *old* migrations, insert a member of each kind and an
old invitation, apply the new migration, and assert the mapping row by row.

R4 — Nothing is lost
No item, board, placement, edge, link, objective or log entry shall change. The migration adds
columns and tables; it does not reshape work.

R5 — Both runtimes
The batch shall run on D1 and on the Node file driver, and the assertion shall be the same in both.

VERIFICATION
V1 — R1: an old owner is an instance admin and a workspace admin; an old member can still edit.
V2 — R2: the documented choice is what the code does — checked by the test, not by the comment.
V3 — R3: the fixture test fails if any mapping line is removed.
V4 — R4: a checksum of every work table is unchanged across the migration.

tasks.title: Every API write checks the role, and reads it live.
tasks.description: Instance and workspace middleware ask can() before a handler runs. No route trusts the session payload, and a role change applies on the next request without re-login.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md sections 3.2, 3.3 and 5.

SCOPE
1. server/access.ts (or server/auth/authorize.ts): the only place authority is resolved.
2. Hono middleware for instance and workspace routes.
3. The session payload the UI may read, clearly marked as data for the UI only.
4. Tests that a viewer cannot write, an editor cannot redesign, and an admin can.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Resolve live
requireUser loads the session user. effectiveInstanceRole and workspaceRole read instance_members and workspace_members on every request. Do not cache the role in the session cookie and do not add a process cache.

R2 - Two guards
requireInstanceAdmin() for /api/admin/*.
requireWorkspace(action) for workspace routes; the workspace id comes from the path, then the body, in a documented order.

R3 - Status
401 when there is no session. 403 when there is one but not the authority. 404 for a resource the caller may not see. 409 for last-administrator and self-protection refusals.

R4 - One answer
The action names passed to the guard are the same Action union from src/domain/roles.ts. There is no second permission table in server code.

R5 - Session payload
GET /api/auth/session returns user (id, name, email, avatarUrl), instanceRole, and workspaces [{ id, role }]. The client uses it to hide controls; the server never trusts it.

R6 - No client authority
A forged body field named role, instanceRole or permissions is ignored, never merged.

R7 - Removal is immediate
Removing a workspace member or changing their role is visible on their next request, with no sign-out required.

TESTS
Two dev identities. Viewer PATCH /api/items/:id -> 403 and no row changes. Editor -> 200 but PUT board design -> 403. Admin -> both. Demote an admin to viewer and repeat without re-login -> 403. Remove a member -> next request 403.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - Viewer write refused at the API, not only hidden in the UI.
V2 - Editor can item.write, cannot board.design.
V3 - Administrator can both.
V4 - A role change takes effect on the next request.
V5 - A removed member loses access on the next request.
V6 - No session payload value can raise the caller's authority.
V7 - A request with no session is 401; a request to a hidden workspace is 404, not 403.

tasks.title: A new instance is closed by default, and the first person is its administrator.
tasks.description: Instance access becomes an explicit setting. A verified address becomes a member only through an invitation, or because the instance is deliberately open; the first arrival owns the instance. This closes the current hole where any verified address joins.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md sections 2 (finding 1) and 3.3 (rules 1-3).

SCOPE
1. An instance settings record: access 'closed' | 'open', default closed.
2. identify() in server/auth/routes.ts respects it.
3. First-run administrator bootstrap, already created by 132; verify it through this path.
4. Admin endpoint and a banner that states the current posture.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Closed by default
When an identity is new and there is no invitation and access is 'closed', sign-in completes at the provider and is then refused with one generic message that does not reveal whether an account or invite exists. No session is issued.

R2 - Open is a decision
With access 'open', a new verified address becomes an instance member and a workspace viewer. It never becomes an administrator. Changing the setting is instance-administrator only and writes an audit event.

R3 - First person
With zero instance_members, the first verified address becomes instance admin and workspace admin in one batch, regardless of the setting. A second person arriving later follows R1.

R4 - Invitations win
An unexpired, unrevoked invitation for the address is accepted before the access check, and gives the invited role.

R5 - Development switch
AUTH_DEV remains a development door, but it follows the same access rule after the first account. The Admin screen and the app shell show a warning whenever it is on.

R6 - No leak
The refusal is identical for an unknown address and an inactive account. Response timing should not distinguish them.

R7 - Surface
GET/PATCH /api/admin/settings reads and writes access. Admin -> Access shows the setting with one sentence of consequence, and the banners in docs/admin.md section 6 appear when the instance is open or the dev switch is on.

TESTS
Closed instance refuses a second verified address; inviting it admits it. Open instance admits it as viewer. First user is admin. A viewer cannot change the setting. A refusal leaves no user, member or session row.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - Closed is the default and refuses an uninvited address after provider verification.
V2 - Open admits a verified address as a viewer, never an administrator.
V3 - The first address becomes instance admin and workspace admin.
V4 - Only an instance admin can toggle access; the change is audited.
V5 - AUTH_DEV cannot bypass closed access after the first account.
V6 - An inactive account and an unknown address receive the same refusal.
V7 - The warning banner renders in the app and in Admin when dev auth is on.

tasks.title: Active and inactive mean one thing everywhere.
tasks.description: An account can be deactivated and reactivated. The switch blocks sign-in, ends every session, hides the person from default pickers, and preserves their history, their assignments and their identity rows so reactivation resumes the same account.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 3.4.

SCOPE
1. status on users, and the two admin routes that change it.
2. One transaction that changes status, revokes sessions and writes audit.
3. The rules that keep the last administrator and the operator from being locked out.
4. Every read surface that must treat an inactive person differently.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Deactivate
POST /api/admin/users/:id/deactivate sets status='inactive', revokes every session in the same batch, and writes one audit event. It answers 204.

R2 - Block
identify() refuses an inactive account before issuing a session, with the same generic refusal as 134. Reactivation restores the same user, the same identities and the same history.

R3 - Preserve
Do not delete identities, memberships, log entries or assignments. A card assigned to an inactive person keeps the assignee; the UI renders the person as inactive and the picker excludes them by default.

R4 - Guards
Extract one guard function used by deactivate, delete, role change and member removal:
- the last active instance administrator cannot be demoted, deactivated, deleted or removed;
- the last active workspace administrator cannot be demoted, removed or deactivated;
- a person cannot deactivate or delete themselves;
- a person cannot demote themselves if it would leave no administrator.
The guard runs before any write and names the reason. It is unit tested independently of HTTP.

R5 - Directory behaviour
Inactive accounts are excluded from the default People list, assignee pickers, mention suggestions and member counts. They remain reachable through the Inactive filter. Their name remains readable on history.

R6 - Invitations
An invitation to an inactive account is not accepted silently; the admin must reactivate it explicitly.

R7 - Audit
Every status change records actor, target and action.

TESTS
Deactivate a user with two live sessions; both stop working. Reactivate; a new sign-in works. Try to deactivate the last administrator and yourself; both 409. Add a second administrator; both are then allowed. Deactivate an assignee; the card still shows them as inactive.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - Inactive cannot sign in and holds no live session.
V2 - Reactivation resumes the same account and history.
V3 - The last administrator cannot be demoted, deactivated, deleted or removed.
V4 - A person cannot deactivate or delete themselves.
V5 - A second administrator makes those operations possible.
V6 - An inactive assignee stays on the card and is excluded from pickers.
V7 - Each status change writes exactly one audit event.

tasks.title: An invitation is a single-use link, not an email row.
tasks.description: Invitations carry a hashed token, an expiry, a role and an inviter. They can be resent and revoked, are accepted once after sign-in by the invited address, and the admin endpoint cannot be used to enumerate accounts.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md sections 3.3 and 5.

SCOPE
1. Token issue, storage, expiry and single use.
2. Admin create/list/resend/revoke.
3. Public inspection and acceptance after sign-in.
4. Tests for replay, forwarding and enumeration.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Token
32 random bytes, base64url. Store only its SHA-256. The plaintext link is returned exactly once, in the create response. Default expiry 14 days; the inviter may choose a shorter one.

R2 - Create
POST /api/admin/invites { email, role } (instance admin). Lowercase the address. If an unexpired invitation already exists for that address, either return 409 or replace it explicitly; do not create two live tokens for one address.

R3 - List and revoke
GET /api/admin/invites returns pending, accepted, expired and revoked, with the inviter and dates. POST /:id/resend issues a new token and kills the old one. DELETE /:id revokes.

R4 - Accept
GET /api/invite/:token is public and says whether the token is valid, its role and a masked address. POST /api/invite/:token requires a session and compares the session's verified email to the invitation address, case-insensitively. A mismatch is 403; used, expired or revoked is 410.

R5 - Write on accept
Create or reuse the user, create instance_members if absent, create workspace_members with the invited role, set accepted_at. All in one batch, plus audit.

R6 - No enumeration
POST /api/admin/invites answers the same status whether or not the address already has an account, and never returns the account details. Token comparison is constant-time.

R7 - No forwarding
A forwarded link still requires sign-in as the invited address to complete; the link alone grants nothing.

TESTS
Create, open in a second browser, sign in as the invited address, accept; membership and role appear. Reuse the link -> 410. Expire it -> 410. Accept as a different verified address -> 403. Resend -> old link 410, new one works. Create for an existing account -> no different response shape.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - The plaintext token is returned once and only a hash is stored.
V2 - A token is single-use; replay returns 410.
V3 - Expiry and revocation are enforced; resend invalidates the previous token.
V4 - A different verified address cannot accept the invitation.
V5 - Acceptance creates the instance and workspace memberships with the invited role.
V6 - The create endpoint does not reveal whether an account exists.
V7 - An old email-only invite cannot be accepted as a link.

tasks.title: A profile the person owns.
tasks.description: Name, avatar, timezone and language are the person's own. Email comes from the verified provider, connected identities are visible, and the page links to the erasure request. There is no password to change.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md sections 3 and 6.

SCOPE
1. GET/PATCH /api/me.
2. Connected identities and unlinking.
3. A Profile screen reachable from the account menu.
4. Avatar handling with a size and type limit.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Fields
The person may change name, avatarUrl, timezone (IANA, validated) and language (ISO 639-1, validated). They may not change email, status, instance role or workspace roles through this endpoint; those fields are ignored, not merged.

R2 - Email
Email is read-only and comes from the verified identity. The UI says so and points at the provider.

R3 - Identities
GET /api/me/identities lists provider, subject and the address each vouches for. DELETE /api/me/identities/:provider/:subject unlinks; refuse to remove the last remaining identity with 409, because that would lock the person out.

R4 - Sessions link
The Profile page shows a summary and links to Security, where sessions live (task 138).

R5 - Erasure
A link to the erasure request (task 126), clearly different from "delete my account", which only an administrator can do.

R6 - UI
The account menu becomes avatar + name, then Profile, Security, Admin (only for an instance administrator), Sign out. It must fail soft with no server, exactly as src/lib/auth.ts does today.

R7 - Limits
Avatar accepts a small image only (reject over 256 KB and anything not image/png, image/jpeg or image/webp). Store as a data URL or a path, matching what src/domain/types.ts User already supports.

TESTS
Patch own name and timezone. Attempt to patch email or role; unchanged. Unlink one of two identities; allowed. Unlink the last; 409. Oversized avatar; 422. Profile page renders with no server and no session.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - A person can change name, avatar, timezone and language.
V2 - Email and roles cannot be changed through /api/me.
V3 - The last identity cannot be unlinked.
V4 - An invalid timezone or language is refused.
V5 - An oversized or non-image avatar is refused.
V6 - The account menu degrades to today's behaviour with no server.

tasks.title: Sessions are visible, revocable, and expire honestly.
tasks.description: Each session records device, a salted address hash and last seen. A person can revoke one or all, an administrator can end a user's sessions, and lifetimes are 12 hours by default and 30 days when remembered.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 3.5.

SCOPE
1. Session metadata and revocation.
2. My Sessions and sign out everywhere.
3. Admin revoke for one user.
4. Cookie and lifetime hardening.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Fields
user_agent, ip_hash (salted with ERROR_SALT, never the raw address), last_seen_at, revoked_at. The token hash remains the primary key.

R2 - Lifetimes
12 hours by default; 30 days when the sign-in asked to be remembered. Store the chosen expiry on the row; do not change the global constant for everyone.

R3 - Last seen
Update last_seen_at on an authenticated request at most once per hour per session, so a busy board does not write on every keystroke.

R4 - My sessions
GET /api/me/sessions returns id (the hash is never returned), device, last seen, created, expiry, current flag. DELETE /api/me/sessions/:id revokes one; revoking the current one is allowed and signs this browser out. POST /api/me/signout-everywhere revokes all.

R5 - Admin
POST /api/admin/users/:id/sessions/revoke revokes all sessions for that user, with audit. Deactivation and deletion already do this in their own transaction.

R6 - Cookie
HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/, Secure whenever PUBLIC_URL is https even if the proxied request arrived over http, and the __Host- prefix in production. Rotate the token on every sign-in.

R7 - Cleanup
An expired or revoked row is refused and may be deleted lazily. A `revoked_at` row is kept long enough to explain a sign-out in the audit window.

TESTS
List two sessions from two user agents. Revoke one; it stops working, the other survives. Sign out everywhere; both stop. Remember-me produces a 30-day expiry, default 12 hours. A forged session id cannot revoke another user's session. Admin revoke ends a user's access without disabling the account.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - A person sees their own sessions and no one else's.
V2 - Revoking one session does not end the others.
V3 - Sign out everywhere ends every session, including the current one.
V4 - Default and remembered lifetimes differ as documented.
V5 - An administrator can revoke a user's sessions; the audit records it.
V6 - A session id from another user is 404, not a successful revoke.
V7 - The cookie has Secure and the production prefix when configured for https.

tasks.title: Every change to access is in the audit log.
tasks.description: One append-only table records sign-ins, refusals, invitations, role changes, deactivations, deletions, imports and share links. It is written by the mutation, not by each handler, and it never stores a token or an address in clear.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 3.6.

SCOPE
1. server/audit.ts with one record() helper.
2. The event list and payload rules.
3. Retention and an index for the screens.
4. Wiring into every access mutation from tasks 133-138.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - One door
record(db, { actorId, action, targetType, targetId, data, ipHash }) is the only writer. A handler does not build SQL for audit itself.

R2 - Events
At least: sign-in succeeded; sign-in refused (inactive, closed, rate-limited); sign-out everywhere; invite created/resent/revoked/accepted; user edited/deactivated/activated/deleted/erased; instance role changed; workspace role granted/changed/revoked; workspace settings changed; board archived; share link created/revoked; import; snapshot restore.

R3 - Payload
`data` is small JSON: changed field names and old/new values for roles and status, never a token, a cookie, a password or a full address. `ip_hash` uses the existing salt.

R4 - Actor
actor_id is the signed-in user, or NULL for a system action (migration, scheduled cleanup). ON DELETE SET NULL keeps the row readable.

R5 - Retention
90 days by default, documented and configurable later. Deleting old rows is one statement and is itself audited once per run, or explicitly exempt with a comment.

R6 - Transaction
The audit write shares the batch with the mutation it describes. A role change that commits without its audit row is a bug; test it.

R7 - Failure
If audit cannot be written, the mutation fails. An access change that cannot be explained afterwards is not worth committing.

TESTS
Each mutation from 134-138 writes exactly one row with the right actor and target. A failed guard writes no success row. No payload contains a token or a raw email. Retention removes only rows older than the window.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - Every access mutation writes exactly one audit event in the same transaction.
V2 - A refused mutation does not write a success event.
V3 - No event contains a token, cookie or raw address.
V4 - An actor who is later deleted leaves a readable event with a NULL actor.
V5 - Retention deletes only rows older than 90 days.
V6 - The audit table is append-only from the application's point of view.

tasks.title: The People screen.
tasks.description: Admin -> People lists every account with role, status, last activity and provider. Its drawer performs edit, role change, deactivate, revoke sessions and delete, and disables the controls that would lock the instance out.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 6. Extend src/components/AdminView.tsx; do not replace the snapshot section, which must remain for the static tier.

SCOPE
1. The list, its filters and its empty states.
2. The person drawer and its actions.
3. The disabled reasons for self and last administrator.
4. The admin-only entry in the account menu.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Access
The section renders only when there is a session and instanceRole is admin. With no server or no session, AdminView shows exactly today's snapshot content and no People section.

R2 - Table
Avatar + name, email, workspace role, status, last active, provider, joined. Search by name and email. Filter by role, status and provider. Sort by name or last active. Server-side pagination with a cursor; no full directory download.

R3 - Drawer
Overview (status, last active, provider, joined), role select with one sentence per role, session summary linking to Security, recent audit for this person, danger zone. Use the existing drawer language rather than a new modal style.

R4 - Actions
Edit name/email; change role; resend invitation when pending; deactivate/activate; revoke sessions; delete; erase. Destructive actions are last, separated, and require typing the email.

R5 - Guardrails
The current user's row has deactivate and delete disabled with a visible reason. The last administrator's role select and removal are disabled with a reason. The server remains the enforcement; the UI only explains.

R6 - Feedback
Every action has a busy state, a success message and a readable failure. A 409 from the guard is shown verbatim, not as "something went wrong".

R7 - Empty and error
No accounts, no matches, and a failed fetch each get their own sentence and a way forward. A 401/403 from the API shows the access explanation, not an empty table.

R8 - Accessibility
Table is a table; the drawer traps focus and closes on Escape; the row menu is keyboard reachable; the role select has a label; status is not conveyed by colour alone.

TESTS
Playwright: admin opens People and sees a member; viewer cannot reach it; deactivate shows the inactive badge and the person disappears from the default filter; last-admin controls are disabled; a 409 is visible; Escape closes the drawer.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - Only an instance administrator sees the People section.
V2 - The static tier still shows only snapshots with no server.
V3 - Search, each filter and each sort change the list.
V4 - Deactivate/activate, role change and revoke sessions work from the drawer.
V5 - Self and last-administrator controls are disabled with a reason.
V6 - Delete and erase require typing the email.
V7 - A 409 from the server is shown as its own sentence.
V8 - Keyboard and screen-reader checks pass for the table, drawer and row menu.

tasks.title: The Invitations screen.
tasks.description: Admin -> Invitations shows pending, accepted, expired and revoked invitations, and issues a copy-once link with a role and an expiry.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 6, "Invite dialog".

SCOPE
1. The list and its states.
2. The create dialog and the copy-once result.
3. Resend and revoke.
4. A test that takes a link through sign-in in a second context.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - List
Group or filter by pending, accepted, expired, revoked. Show address, role, inviter, created, expires, accepted. A pending row says how long is left in words.

R2 - Create
Email, role (Viewer / Editor / Administrator with one sentence each), expiry (default 14 days). On success, a dialog shows the full link with a Copy button and the sentence "This link is shown once." Closing it cannot recover the link; the remedy is resend.

R3 - Resend and revoke
Resend asks for confirmation because it invalidates the old link. Revoke is immediate and confirmed. Both show the resulting state without a reload.

R4 - Accept visibility
When an invitation is accepted, the row moves to Accepted with the time and the account name; it never disappears, because the record of who invited whom is useful.

R5 - No email dependency
The flow must complete by copying a link. Sending email later is additive and must not be required to build or test this screen.

R6 - Safety
The create endpoint's 204-for-everything behaviour is reflected in the UI: the dialog does not say "that address already has an account".

R7 - Accessibility
Copy is a real button with a live-region announcement; the link field is selectable; the result dialog traps focus and can be dismissed with Escape.

TESTS
Create a Viewer invitation, copy the link, sign in as that address in a second browser context, accept, and see Accepted in the list. Revoke a second invitation and confirm the link is refused. Resend and confirm the old link is dead. Create for an existing account and confirm the UI says nothing different.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - The four invitation states are visible and filterable.
V2 - The created link is shown once and copied with a button.
V3 - Resend invalidates the old link; revoke prevents acceptance.
V4 - Accepting moves the row to Accepted with the account.
V5 - The screen works without email delivery.
V6 - The UI does not reveal whether an address already has an account.
V7 - The result dialog and copy control are keyboard accessible.

tasks.title: Workspace members and their roles.
tasks.description: A workspace administrator can see every member, change a role, remove a member and invite someone directly into the workspace, with the last-administrator rule enforced.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md sections 3.1-3.3 and 5.

SCOPE
1. Admin -> Workspace: name, description and member list.
2. Role change, removal and direct invitation.
3. The boundary between instance administration and workspace administration.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Who may see it
A workspace administrator sees this section for their workspace. An instance administrator may see any workspace by virtue of the bypass. An ordinary editor or viewer does not see it.

R2 - Member list
Name, avatar, role, status, joined. Role select with the three roles and a one-line consequence. Removal is separate from deactivation: removal ends access to this workspace and leaves the instance account alone.

R3 - Invite into a workspace
Email plus workspace role; uses the token flow from 136. The invitation says which workspace it is for. An instance-level invite and a workspace invite are distinguishable in the list.

R4 - Guards
The last active workspace administrator cannot be demoted or removed. A person may leave only if another administrator remains. The guard runs before the write and returns 409 with a reason.

R5 - Effect
A role change or removal applies on the next request. The UI says so in one sentence rather than promising a live update.

R6 - No escalation
A workspace administrator cannot grant themselves instance admin, and cannot change roles in a workspace they do not administer.

R7 - Shared component
The role select and guard explanation are reused by the People drawer (140) rather than duplicated.

TESTS
Invite a viewer into a workspace, accept, and see them listed. Promote to editor; they can write on the next request. Remove; next request 403. Try to demote the last workspace admin; 409. A workspace admin cannot change another workspace's members.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - Only a workspace administrator or instance administrator sees the section.
V2 - Role change is effective on the next request.
V3 - Removal ends workspace access but not the instance account.
V4 - The last workspace administrator cannot be demoted or removed.
V5 - A workspace invitation names its workspace and grants the invited role.
V6 - No workspace administrator can escalate to instance administrator.
V7 - The role select and guard copy match the People screen.

tasks.title: Admin -> Audit and Health.
tasks.description: The audit log is readable and filterable, and the health page shows database status, build, the error inbox, and the banners that say when an instance is not locked down.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 6 and README's error-report section (the screen task 107 promised).

SCOPE
1. Admin -> Audit: filter, pagination, detail.
2. Admin -> Health: /api/health, build, error inbox, posture banners.
3. Scope: instance admin reads all; workspace admin reads their workspace.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Audit list
Newest first, cursor paged. Filter by actor, action, target type/id and date range. Each row reads as a sentence ("Maya changed Priya's role from Viewer to Editor"), with the raw action available on the detail. No JSON dump as the primary view.

R2 - Audit scope
An instance administrator reads every event. A workspace administrator reads events whose target belongs to their workspace and never instance-level events. A viewer sees none of it.

R3 - Health
Database reachable (already /api/health), build version and commit, the error inbox from the errors table, and counts of accounts, inactive accounts and administrators.

R4 - Error inbox
List newest first with message, path, view, build, time and a detail view for the stack. This is the read side of task 107. No query string and no raw address are shown, because they were never stored.

R5 - Posture
Banners for open instance, AUTH_DEV on, and no provider configured. Each links to the relevant setting or documentation.

R6 - Retention
The audit page states its 90-day window. The error inbox states its hourly cap.

R7 - No new data
This task reads existing tables. It must not add analytics, tracking or a third-party service.

TESTS
Viewer cannot reach either page. Workspace admin sees only their workspace events. Date and actor filters narrow the list. Error detail shows the stack. The correct banner appears when the corresponding setting or env var is on. Counts match the People list.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - Audit and Health are reachable only by the right authority.
V2 - Audit filters and pagination work; a workspace admin sees only their workspace.
V3 - Each audit row reads as a sentence.
V4 - The error inbox lists and opens a report without revealing a query or address.
V5 - Counts on Health match the directory.
V6 - Posture banners reflect the live configuration.
V7 - No analytics or third-party request is introduced.

tasks.title: Delete and erase are different promises.
tasks.description: Deleting an account removes the person and their sessions but leaves their history readable. Erasing removes personal data but keeps the id so the log and assignments survive. The two are separate buttons with different copy.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 3.4 and task 126's data promise.

SCOPE
1. DELETE /api/admin/users/:id.
2. POST /api/admin/users/:id/erase.
3. The confirmations and the history rendering.
4. Tests that history survives both.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Delete
One batch removes sessions, identities, instance_members and workspace_members, then the user row. It does not touch items, log entries, placements, dependencies or audit events. The operation is refused for self and the last administrator.

R2 - History after delete
A log entry whose `by` no longer resolves renders "Former member"; the existing optional `by` in src/domain/types.ts already allows this. A card assigned to the deleted person keeps a ghost assignee until someone reassigns it, and the card says so.

R3 - Erase
Replace name with "Former member", email with a per-user opaque value or empty string, avatar with null. Delete identities and sessions. Keep the user id and the log's `by` so referential integrity and history survive. Instance and workspace memberships are removed. One audit event records the erasure, with no personal data in it.

R4 - Request flow
Task 126 owns the user-facing request and the copy. This task owns the mechanics and links to that flow. A request is not the same as an administrator's immediate action; the UI distinguishes them.

R5 - Confirmation
Both require typing the account's email. The dialog explains the difference in one sentence each: delete frees the address and keeps the work's history under "Former member"; erase removes the personal data and keeps the work.

R6 - Re-invitation
After delete, the same address may be invited again and becomes a new account. After erase, the address is free but the old id remains as a history anchor.

R7 - Audit
Both write an event; the erased event does not contain the old name or address.

TESTS
Delete a user who authored a log entry and was assigned a card: the log reads "Former member", the card still names a ghost, the address can be invited again. Erase: the email is gone from users and identities, the id still resolves the log, the audit event has no PII. Self and last-admin refusals hold.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - Delete removes the account, identities, sessions and memberships.
V2 - Delete leaves log entries and assignments readable as "Former member".
V3 - Erase removes name, email and avatar but keeps the id.
V4 - Erase deletes identities and sessions and writes an audit event with no PII.
V5 - Both refuse self and the last administrator.
V6 - The confirmation requires typing the email and explains the difference.
V7 - A deleted address can be invited again; an erased id still anchors history.

tasks.title: The conveniences: allowed domains, bulk actions and CSV.
tasks.description: An instance can admit a verified company domain instead of inviting one by one, the people list can act on a selection, and the directory exports as CSV.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md sections 3.3 and 7 (P2).

SCOPE
1. allowed_domains as an instance setting, evaluated in identify().
2. Bulk deactivate/activate and bulk role change, judged before writing.
3. CSV export of the directory.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Domains
A list of lowercase domains, e.g. example.com. A verified address whose domain matches exactly is admitted under the current access rules (closed means only existing members and invites; the domain list is an explicit third door). It becomes a Viewer, never an administrator. No suffix or substring matching: notexample.com must not match example.com.

R2 - Domain UI
Admin -> Access edits the list, explains the role granted, and warns that it is an access door. Changes are audited. An empty list changes nothing.

R3 - Bulk
The People list can select many rows and deactivate, activate or change role. The whole selection is judged before anything is written, the way setParents refuses a selection that would cycle: if any row is the last administrator, the operator themselves, or would leave no administrator, the whole operation is refused and the row is named. No partial application.

R4 - Bulk feedback
The result says how many changed and names any refusal. No optimistic UI that later rolls back.

R5 - CSV
Export name, email, workspace role, status, last active, joined. No sessions, tokens or IP hashes. A header row and RFC 4180 quoting. The file name carries the date.

R6 - Scale
A selection and an export are server-side; do not load the whole directory to render a page.

TESTS
Admit a user from an allowed domain, then one from a lookalike domain; only the first is admitted, as Viewer. Bulk deactivate a selection containing the last admin; nothing changes. Export and re-read the CSV: columns, quoting and no secret fields.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - An allowed domain admits a verified address as Viewer only.
V2 - A lookalike domain does not match.
V3 - The domain list is visible and audited.
V4 - A bulk operation refuses as a whole when one row is protected.
V5 - Bulk success reports the number changed.
V6 - CSV has the documented columns, correct quoting and no secrets.
V7 - Page and export are server-side and do not download the directory.

tasks.title: Groups: a role granted once to many.
tasks.description: A group is a named set of users so a workspace role is granted once. Inactive groups grant nothing. This is deliberately deferred until there is more than one workspace and a customer asks for it.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 3.1 (the v1 decision) and section 7 (P3).

SCOPE
1. groups and group_members tables.
2. group_workspace_roles, joining the existing workspace_members permission check.
3. Active/inactive groups.
4. Admin UI, behind the same instance-admin door.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Model
groups(id, name, description, active, created_by, created_at). group_members(group_id, user_id, added_by, added_at). group_workspace_roles(group_id, workspace_id, role).

R2 - Effective role
A person's workspace role is the union of their direct workspace_members row and every active group role. The highest role wins. The guard function names the source (direct or group) so the UI can explain it.

R3 - Inactive group
Grants nothing, immediately. Its members keep any direct role.

R4 - Last administrator
A group granting admin counts toward the last-administrator calculation. Removing the last admin-bearing group assignment is refused just like removing the last person.

R5 - No recursion
Groups do not nest. Add nesting only with a cycle guard and a real requirement.

R6 - Versioning
Every assignment and membership change is audited.

TESTS
Two people in a group with Editor can edit. Deactivate the group; both lose Editor but keep a direct Viewer. Removing the last admin group is refused. A group role cannot exceed the assigning administrator's authority.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - A group role applies to every active member.
V2 - An inactive group grants nothing.
V3 - The highest direct or group role wins.
V4 - The last administrator rule counts group-granted admins.
V5 - Groups do not nest, or nesting is cycle-safe.
V6 - Every change is audited.

tasks.title: A custom role label that grants nothing.
tasks.description: An administrator can name a role for routing approvals or describing a team, but the label carries no permissions. Windshift's deliberate choice, and the only safe way to offer custom roles.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md section 8 (custom roles).

SCOPE
1. A label entity, separate from the permission role.
2. Assignment to a person, per workspace.
3. No permission path from the label.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Separate fields
workspace_members.role stays the closed set. A new custom_label_id (nullable) or a separate person_labels table carries the display name. It is never read by can().

R2 - Label only
The UI shows the label beside the role, and says in one sentence that it does not grant access. Creating, renaming and deleting labels is workspace-administrator work.

R3 - No escalation by naming
A label called "Administrator" grants nothing. The permission role is the only authority. Test this by naming a label Administrator and confirming a viewer stays a viewer.

R4 - Deletion
Deleting a label does not remove anyone's permission role and does not delete a person.

R5 - Audit
Label assignment and removal are audited, because they route people.

TESTS
Create a label called Administrator, assign it to a Viewer; every write is still 403. Delete the label; the person's role is unchanged. A label cannot be used in the role guard.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - A custom label is never consulted by can().
V2 - A label named Administrator grants no authority.
V3 - Deleting a label leaves roles and accounts intact.
V4 - Assignment and removal are audited.
V5 - Only a workspace administrator manages labels.

tasks.title: API tokens with scopes.
tasks.description: A person can mint a token for a script or an agent, choose its scopes and expiry, see it once, and revoke it. Deferred until there is an API worth calling.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md sections 5 and 8.

SCOPE
1. api_tokens table: id, user_id, name, token_hash, scopes, expires_at, last_used_at, revoked_at.
2. Create/list/revoke endpoints and a Security page section.
3. Scope enforcement on the API routes that exist.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Secret handling
32 random bytes, shown once, stored as SHA-256. Never logged, never returned by list, never in audit data.

R2 - Scopes
resource:action strings, at least boards:read, boards:write, items:read, items:write, admin:users:read. A token can never exceed its owner's role: both the scope and the role are checked.

R3 - Expiry
Optional expiry, default 90 days. An expired or revoked token is 401 on the next request.

R4 - Identity
A token authenticates as its owner. Its last_used_at updates at most hourly. The UI shows the last use and a Revoke button.

R5 - Admin visibility
An instance administrator can list and revoke tokens for an account in the People drawer, with audit. The token value is never available to the administrator.

R6 - No privilege escalation
Minting a token with a scope the owner's role cannot exercise is refused at mint time, not silently at use.

TESTS
Mint a read-only token; write is 403, read is 200. Revoke; next request 401. Expire; 401. A viewer cannot mint an items:write token. A list response never contains a token or hash. Admin revoke is audited.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - The token is shown once and only a hash is stored.
V2 - Scope and role are both enforced.
V3 - An expired or revoked token is 401.
V4 - A token cannot exceed its owner's authority.
V5 - Listing never reveals a token or hash.
V6 - An administrator can revoke but never read a token.
V7 - Admin revocation is audited.

tasks.title: A second factor, if a deployment ever needs one.
tasks.description: Deferred. OAuth/OIDC is the only door today, and adding a second factor means adding a credential the provider does not hold. This task records the trigger and the shape so the decision is not reopened from scratch.
tasks.details:
SYSTEM
Flowline. Read docs/admin.md sections 1.4 and 8.

SCOPE
1. An instance policy: provider only (default), or provider plus a registered second factor.
2. WebAuthn registration and verification for the second factor.
3. Recovery, or an explicit administrator fallback.

REQUIREMENTS

R1 - Trigger
Do not build this until a real deployment requires it. The provider's own MFA already covers most teams and costs nothing to support.

R2 - Policy
One instance-wide policy with preview mode, as Windshift does: warn first, enforce later, list affected users before enforcing.

R3 - Credential
WebAuthn only. No TOTP secret, no password, no SSH key, because none of those exist elsewhere in Flowline.

R4 - Recovery
An administrator fallback that is explicitly enabled, audited, and shown as a banner while it is on. Losing the only factor must not lock the last administrator out permanently.

R5 - Sessions
A second-factor change revokes other sessions and writes audit.

TESTS
Preview mode warns without blocking. Enforced mode refuses a session without the factor. Recovery works only when enabled and is audited. The last administrator cannot enrol into a state with no recovery path.
tasks.testStrategy:
VERIFICATION

V1 - The default policy is provider-only and changes nothing today.
V2 - Preview warns; enforce blocks.
V3 - Only WebAuthn is accepted as the second factor.
V4 - Recovery is explicit, audited and bannered.
V5 - Enrolment revokes other sessions.
V6 - The last administrator cannot be locked out.
